faq.a: A lodestone is a naturally magnetised piece of magnetite, an iron-rich mineral. It attracts iron and was the first magnet people knew about.

faq.q: Why is lightning thought to magnetise lodestones?
faq.a: Lodestones are found near the surface, not deep underground, and their magnetism is often strongest in patches. That pattern matches the brief, intense magnetic field of a lightning strike, which is far stronger than Earth's own field.
asks: How does a rock become magnetic?

faq.a: Domains are tiny regions inside a magnetic material where the atoms' little magnets all point the same way. When most domains line up together, the whole object acts as a magnet.

faq.q: How were lodestones used as compasses?
faq.a: A lodestone, or a needle rubbed on one, swings to line up with Earth's magnetic field when it can turn freely. In ancient China, spoon-shaped lodestones on a smooth plate pointed the way, and later magnetised needles guided sailors.

faq.q: Where does the word magnet come from?
faq.a: It comes from Magnesia, a region of ancient Greece where magnetic stones were found. The word lodestone means leading stone, because it was used to lead travellers the right way.
asks: Why is it called a lodestone?

facts: Magnetite, the mineral of lodestone, is an iron oxide with the formula Fe3O4.
Lode is an old English word for way or journey, so lodestone means leading stone.

quiz.say: What most likely turned an ordinary lump of magnetite into a strong lodestone?
quiz.show: A lodestone was most likely magnetised by…
quiz.why: A lightning strike's huge current makes a brief, very strong magnetic field that lines up the magnetic domains in the rock.

wrong.0: Sunlight doesn't line up magnetic domains; heating actually weakens magnets.
wrong.2: Water has no effect on a rock's magnetism.
